The sound of high energy

A Spotify track study on musical mood, loudness, and what changes when you compare within genre

Two Spotify tags can describe similarly energetic tracks while landing in very different places on the mood scale. And a single loudness comparison can change by more than a decibel depending on which genres are included. Both stories start with the unit of analysis: a track ID within a genre, or a track ID counted once across the sample.

Similar energy, different valence

Energy is Spotify’s estimate of intensity and activity. Valence is its estimate of musical positivity. Read across the top of the chart: hardstyle and the party label have similar energy, but party scores much higher on valence. Salsa has the highest valence median in this sample at a lower energy level. Each dot is a genre median. Spotify audio-feature definitions.

Across 48,070 tracks with energy of at least 0.65, 29% fall into the shaded low-valence area. The contrast between hardstyle and party also holds inside a tighter energy band. Among tracks with energy from 0.85 to 0.95, 65% of the hardstyle tracks score below 0.35 on valence (448 tracks in the band), compared with 5% for party (374 tracks in the band). Near the middle of both scales, Soul has median valence 0.512 and energy 0.525. Pop has nearly the same median valence (0.499) and sits higher on energy (0.618).

What the dataset calls happy

The dataset uses happy as a genre tag. That bucket contains tracks by Scooter, The Prophet, and Darren Styles. The publisher describes the column as genre and gives the valence score in a separate audio-feature column. The individual scores can also vary widely within the same tag and artist. Dataset column definitions.

The median valence of the happy tag is 0.274. Two Scooter tracks under that tag illustrate the spread. Nessaja scores 0.104 on valence and How Much Is The Fish? scores 0.681. Both have energy above 0.90. Valence is a separate estimate of the sound. Listeners may hear the tracks differently. Listen to Nessaja · Listen to How Much Is The Fish?

Why the explicit-track loudness gap shrinks

Across the full sample, explicit tracks are about 2 dB louder on average. The chart compares two pools: all distinct track IDs, and the distinct track IDs with at least one qualifying genre label. In each pool, we average the explicit tracks and non-explicit tracks separately.

The gap goes from 2.03 dB to 0.62 dB. The non-explicit average rises by 1.43 dB as 38,451 non-explicit tracks leave the pool (their mean is -10.30 dB). The explicit average moves by only 0.02 dB, with 294 explicit tracks outside the qualifying labels. So most of the change comes from which tracks are in the non-explicit group.

Which genre labels qualify?

Check each existing Spotify label separately. Count each track ID once within that label. The label qualifies if it has at least 30 explicit tracks and at least 30 non-explicit tracks. The cutoff gives both group averages a minimum number of tracks. It is an analysis choice and the result can depend on it.

A track with several genre labels stays in the restricted pool if any of its labels qualifies. Every track in that pool contributes once to its group’s overall average. For the separate within-label calculation, the same track can contribute to each of its qualifying labels.

66 of 114 labels qualify. Of the 48 excluded labels, 48 fall below 30 explicit tracks (8 have zero), and 0 fall below 30 non-explicit tracks.

What happens within a label?

With each label weighted equally, explicit tracks average 0.92 dB louder. In 13 of 66 labels the gap goes the other way, including emo (-1.62 dB) and hip-hop (-0.24 dB). The median label gap is +0.72 dB.

Dataset and counting rules

The Spotify Tracks Dataset on Kaggle was collected from the Spotify Web API. Each label starts with the same number of rows, so genre frequency reflects how the dataset was assembled. Spotify’s popularity field is a snapshot score. The CSV has no release dates or per-track play counts.

The CSV has 114,000 rows across 114 labels (1,000 rows per label). Cleaning removes 1 incomplete rows and 450 extra rows within track-and-label pairs. 16,299 IDs appear under multiple labels. A track ID identifies a Spotify version, so a recording may still appear under different IDs.
